procedural_history.originating_court: Special Tribunal (located at Lahore, constituted by Ordinance No. 29 of 1943)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated March 21, 1962, of the Punjab High Court in Criminal Appeals Nos. 478 and 479, and 41, 176, 478 and 479 of 1949.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Special Tribunal convicted the appellant on all ten charges. On appeal, the Punjab High Court upheld the conviction in respect of part of charge No. 21, charge No. 22, and charge No. 26, but acquitted him of the rest. The High Court also dealt with issues regarding the examination of witnesses in Burma and Pakistan, and the provision of funds for the appellant's defense.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant filed two appeals (Nos. 150 & 151/1962) in the Supreme Court against the High Court's upholding of his conviction on part of charge No. 21, charge No. 22, and charge No. 26. The State filed four appeals (Nos. 196 to 199 of 1962) against the High Court's orders of acquittal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant was wrongly convicted as the offence of cheating had not been made out against him.

facts: The appellant, a contractor, was convicted of cheating under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code for submitting bogus claims for payment to the Government of Burma.
The appellant raised three main arguments to challenge his conviction:
1. The government's payments were not a result of his false claims, but rather of the incorrect verification reports submitted by other officers.
2. He lacked personal knowledge that the claims were bogus, particularly for work allegedly done after he had already left Burma.

3. Even if guilty, the offense should be under Section 417 (simple cheating) and not Section 420, because the crime was complete when the payment was sanctioned, not when the money was later delivered.
law: Cheating under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code involves dishonestly inducing a person to deliver property.
The offense is not complete until the property is delivered.
A person's knowledge, being a state of mind, does not require direct evidence and can be inferred from the facts and circumstances of the case.
application: The Court rejected the argument that the officers' reports broke the chain of causation. It held that the entire process, from the appellant's initial false representations to the final payment, constituted a single transaction. The payments were the culmination of the appellant's act of putting forward bogus claims.

The Court dismissed the claim of lack of knowledge. It reasoned that since the High Court had factually determined that the work was never done at all, the very fact that the claims were bogus led to the inference that the appellant knew they were false. The Court also noted the appellant failed to provide any explanation that he was acting on information from someone else.

The Court also rejected the distinction between Section 417 and 420 in this case. It stated that the transaction was not complete merely when the sanction orders were passed. The subsequent delivery of money was part of the same transaction initiated by the false claims, making the conviction under Section 420 appropriate.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's arguments and affirmed his conviction for cheating under Section 420. The Court found that the appellant's false claims were the direct cause of the government parting with its money, that the entire process was a single transaction correctly charged under Section 420, and that his knowledge of the falsity of the claims could be properly inferred from the circumstances.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Special Tribunal was incompetent to hold the trials on the ground that the ordinance under which it was constituted had expired after six months, rendering subsequent extensions invalid.

facts: The appellant challenged the validity of the trials, arguing that the Special Tribunal was incompetent.
The argument was that the Tribunal was constituted under Ordinance No. 29 of 1943, which was issued under s. 72 of the Ninth Schedule of the Government of India Act, 1935.
Section 72 stipulated that such an ordinance would only remain in force for a maximum of six months.

Therefore, the appellant claimed the ordinance expired six months after its promulgation on September 9, 1943, making the Tribunal defunct and rendering subsequent extensions by other ordinances and acts invalid.
law: The Court identified that the appellant's argument ignored a key piece of legislation: s. 1(3) of the India and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940.
This Act suspended the operation of the clause in s. 72 of the Government of India Act that limited an ordinance's life to six months.

The Court cited a Federal Court precedent, J. K. Gas Plant Manufacturing Co. v. The King Emperor, which had already held that this specific Ordinance (29/1943) did not expire after six months but remained in force until September 30, 1946.
application: Applying the law, the Court found that the six-month limitation did not apply to Ordinance 29 of 1943.
The Tribunal constituted under this ordinance was therefore functioning competently until September 30, 1946.
On the very next day, October 1, 1946, the Punjab Ordinance III of 1946 came into force, which continued the powers of the Tribunal without any interruption.
This was subsequently replaced by Punjab Act X of 1950, which further continued the Tribunal's existence and powers.
The Court concluded that there was a seamless and uninterrupted legal basis for the Tribunal's functioning throughout the trials.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the Special Tribunal was competent. The Court reasoned that the six-month expiry rule for the original ordinance was suspended by the India and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940. The Tribunal's authority was validly and continuously extended by subsequent legislation without any break, ensuring it was properly constituted at all stages of the trial.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Special Tribunal was improperly constituted due to changes in its membership over time.

facts: The Special Tribunal was initially constituted by the Central Government with three members under Ordinance No. 29 of 1943.
In 1947, one member died and the President of the Tribunal left India, reducing the membership to one.
Subsequently, the Punjab Government appointed two new members to the Tribunal.
Later, the law was changed by Punjab Act X of 1950, which provided that the Tribunal would be composed of only one member instead of three.
law: Under Ordinance No. 29 of 1943, the power to constitute the Special Tribunal was vested in the Central Government.

Punjab Ordinance III of 1946 continued the Tribunal's existence and, under its Section 3(3), gave the Punjab Government the power to "supersede or modify" notifications that had been issued by the Central Government.
Punjab Act X of 1950 altered the required composition of the Special Tribunal from three members to one.
application: The appellant argued that the Punjab Government did not have the authority to appoint new members, as this power was not explicitly transferred to it from the Central Government.

The Court rejected this argument, reasoning that the appointment of new members by the Punjab Government was a valid exercise of its power to "modify" the original notification by which the Central Government had constituted the Tribunal. This power was granted by Section 3(3) of the Punjab Ordinance.
The Court noted that during the period when the Tribunal was temporarily reduced to one member (when the law required three), no trial proceedings were conducted against the appellant.
The Court also found that when the Tribunal later functioned with a single member, it was legally valid because the law had been amended by Punjab Act X of 1950 to permit a one-member Tribunal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Special Tribunal was properly constituted at each stage of the proceedings. The Punjab Government had the authority to appoint new members, and the trial was only conducted when the Tribunal's composition met the legal requirements of the time. Therefore, the Court rejected the appellant's challenge to the Tribunal's constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court committed an error of law in acquitting the appellant of certain charges, thereby justifying interference by the Supreme Court in the State's appeals.

facts: The appellant was acquitted by the High Court on several charges.
The State of Punjab filed four appeals against these orders of acquittal.
The High Court's reason for acquittal was its finding of fact that the prosecution had failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the claims paid to the appellant were bogus.
law: The Supreme Court will only interfere with findings of fact recorded by a High Court if an error of law has been committed.
application: The Supreme Court examined the State's appeals and found that the counsel for the State was unable to demonstrate that the High Court had committed any error of law.
The High Court's decision to acquit was based on a finding of fact regarding the prosecution's failure to meet its burden of proof.
Since no error of law was shown in the High Court's factual findings, the standard for interference by the Supreme Court was not met.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the State's appeals, concluding that the findings of fact recorded by the High Court did not call for any interference because the State failed to show that any error of law had been committed by the High Court in acquitting the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Whether the trial was vitiated by the authorities' failure to provide adequate funds for the appellant's defence, specifically for examining witnesses in Burma.

facts: The appellant claimed his trial was prejudiced because he was not given adequate funds to examine defence witnesses in Burma.
The appellant's properties and funds had been attached under Ordinance 38 of 1944.
Under this Ordinance, the District Judge was to provide reasonably necessary funds for defence from the attached property.
The District Judge directed a payment of Rs. 3,000/- for the examination of witnesses in Burma.
The High Court found that this payment, along with others for maintenance, had completely exhausted all of the appellant's attached funds.
While steps were being taken to facilitate the examination of witnesses (including renewing the appellant's passport), the appellant himself withdrew his request to have the witnesses examined.
law: Ordinance 38 of 1944, Section 9, required the District Judge to provide funds for the defence of the applicant from the attached property in which the applicant claimed an interest.
application: The Court first determined that there was no refusal by the authorities to provide funds to which the appellant was entitled. The authorities had provided Rs. 3,000/- from the appellant's attached property, and the High Court had confirmed that these funds were completely exhausted. Therefore, no more money was legally available to be paid.
More importantly, the Court found that the entire grievance about the non-provision of funds was "immaterial."
The reason it was immaterial was that the appellant, of his own accord, ultimately withdrew his request for the examination of the witnesses in Burma.
Because the appellant himself abandoned the request, the Court concluded that there had been no denial of his right to produce the defence he desired.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the trial was not vitiated. The Court reasoned that, firstly, the authorities had provided all the funds that were legally available from the appellant's attached property, and secondly, the issue was rendered moot because the appellant himself withdrew his request to examine the witnesses in Burma.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant was wrongly convicted as the offence of cheating had not been made out against him.
appellant_arguments: The payments made to the appellant were not a result of his representations but were based on the verification reports submitted by various officers.
If any offence of cheating was committed, it was by the officers who submitted the wrong verification reports, not by the appellant.
respondent_arguments: The payments made to the appellant were directly connected with and induced by the representations made by the appellant in his bills.
The officers who verified the bogus bills could be guilty of abetting, but this does not absolve the appellant from the primary offence of cheating initiated by his false claims.

cases.case_name: Sarwant Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: The legal principle is not stated in the provided text.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An offence constitutes cheating with delivery of property under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code even if the victim decides to part with the property at one point in time and the actual delivery happens subsequently; the offence is not reduced to simple cheating under Section 417 merely because of this time gap. Additionally, diaries maintained under army rules are admissible as records of official acts under Section 35 of the Evidence Act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant was guilty of cheating because his false representations in the submitted bills were the direct and ultimate cause of the government making payments to satisfy those claims. The fact that government officers may have abetted the crime by wrongly verifying the bills does not absolve the appellant of the primary offence. Separately, the High Court's acquittal of the appellant on other charges was based on findings of fact, and the State failed to demonstrate any error of law that would justify interference by the Supreme Court.
legal_tests_applied: For an offence of cheating, the critical test is whether the payments were 'connected with or induced by the representations made by the appellant himself or in his bills.'

For the Supreme Court to interfere with a High Court's findings of fact in an appeal against acquittal, the appellant (the State in this instance) must demonstrate that an 'error of law has been committed by the High Court.'
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that the verifying officers' reports, rather than the appellant's claims, induced the payment, finding that 'it were those representations by the appellant which ultimately cnlminated in the Government of Burma parting with the money to satisfy those claims put forward by the appellant.'
The potential guilt of the verifying officers for abetment does not negate the appellant's primary role in the offence of cheating.

Regarding the State's appeals against his acquittal on other charges, the appellant (as respondent) prevailed because the State was unable 'to show to us that any error of law has been committed by the High Court when recording findings of fact.'
why_respondent_won: The State successfully established the offence of cheating by showing that the payments 'were not connected with or induced by the representations made by the appellant himself or in his bills.'
The High Court's findings of fact in the matters where it acquitted the appellant were upheld because they did 'not, therefore, call for any interference by this Court' as no error of law was shown.
